stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion of Leyla Demir's team in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Excavating a hilltop site in central Anatolia, archaeologist Leyla Demir's team recovered charred barley from several hearths that radiocarbon dating places around 6,800 years ago. Because barley must be planted and tended, the team concluded that the hilltop held a permanent farming village.

Text 2
Grain is easy to carry, however. Mobile herders who traded with lowland farmers could have cooked barley at a seasonal camp and left the same charred remains. Until excavators find storage pits or durable houses, calling the hilltop a year-round village is premature.
choices: By arguing that the charred barley does not by itself show that people lived on the hilltop year-round
By arguing that the charred barley proves the hilltop was used only by herders during part of the year
By arguing that the radiocarbon dates for the hearths are likely to be several centuries too early
By arguing that the charred barley confirms that farmers planted and tended crops on the hilltop
explanation: Text 1 ends on its conclusion: the hilltop was a permanent farming village. Text 2 doesn't deny that the barley was found. It says herders could have left the same remains, so calling the site a village is "premature." That means the evidence hasn't shown the claim, which is exactly what this choice says.

B.why: You took Text 2's alternative for proof. Text 2 says herders "could have" left the barley and that the question is still open. It never says herders definitely used the site.

C.why: You aimed Text 2's doubt at a side detail. Text 2 never questions the radiocarbon dates. Its objection is to what the barley says about permanent settlement.

D.why: You reversed Text 2's position. Text 2 suggests the barley may have been brought in from lowland farms, so it would not accept that the barley shows crops were grown on the hilltop.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the planners' conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In 2023, the city of Marlow painted protected bike lanes along Fenner Avenue. A year later, automated counters recorded 40 percent more cyclists on the avenue than before. City planners concluded that the new lanes had persuaded many residents to start cycling.

Text 2
Although the rise on Fenner Avenue is real, it may not reflect new riders. Cyclists who once used the parallel side streets could simply have moved to the safer avenue. Counters on those side streets would show whether the total number of cyclists actually grew.
choices: By claiming that the protected lanes have reduced the total number of cyclists across Marlow
By claiming that the protected lanes on Fenner Avenue were too costly for the city to build
By claiming that the increase may come from existing cyclists changing routes, not new ones
By claiming that the counters on Fenner Avenue did not record any real increase in cyclists
explanation: The planners concluded that the lanes created new cyclists. Text 2 accepts that the count went up ("the rise... is real"). It gives a different explanation: riders may have moved over from side streets. This choice matches that stance and aims it at the planners' conclusion.

A.why: You went further than Text 2 does. Text 2 only says the total may not have grown and that more counting is needed. It never says cycling fell.

B.why: You picked an objection Text 2 never makes. Cost isn't mentioned. Text 2's response is about what explains the higher count.

D.why: You missed the concession. Text 2 says the rise "is real," so it accepts the counter data and questions only how to interpret it.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the agency's conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
After decades of heavy pumping, water levels in the Corrin Valley aquifer had fallen steadily. Following an unusually wet winter, however, monitoring wells across the valley showed levels rising by up to two meters. The regional water agency therefore announced that the aquifer has recovered.

Text 2
The wells that rose are shallow, and they tap only the aquifer's upper layer, which refills quickly after heavy rain. Wells reaching the deep layer, where most of the pumped water came from, showed no change. One wet winter does not mean the whole aquifer has recovered.
choices: By insisting that water levels in the shallow wells actually fell during the wet winter
By insisting that the rise in shallow wells does not show that the entire aquifer recovered
By insisting that the deep layer is now emptier than it was before the wet winter began
By insisting that the agency measured the winter's rainfall in the valley incorrectly
explanation: Text 1 ends with the agency's claim that the aquifer has recovered. Text 2 narrows that claim. The shallow layer did rise, but the deep layer, where most of the pumping happened, didn't change. So the evidence does not show that the whole aquifer recovered.

A.why: You reversed a fact both texts accept. Text 2 agrees the shallow wells rose and explains why they refill quickly.

C.why: You made Text 2 stronger than it is. Text 2 says the deep wells "showed no change." It never says the deep layer got worse.

D.why: You aimed Text 2's doubt at a detail neither text discusses. Text 2 has no complaint about rainfall measurement. Its point is about which layer of the aquifer rose.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Okafor's conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a set of twelve eighteenth-century woodcut landscapes, the sky darkens unevenly, with ink thick near the top edge and fading toward the horizon. Art historian Daniel Okafor argues that this unevenness shows the printer was an inexperienced apprentice who could not yet ink a block smoothly.

Text 2
Okafor's reading seems unlikely. Some woodcut workshops deliberately wiped ink from part of a block before printing to make skies fade gradually. The same pattern appearing in all twelve prints points to a chosen technique rather than an unsteady hand.
choices: By suggesting that the ink in the twelve skies is actually spread evenly from top to bottom
By suggesting that the twelve landscapes were printed on paper made much later than assumed
By suggesting that the printer must have been the most highly skilled artisan in the workshop
By suggesting that the uneven skies more likely reflect a deliberate method than inexperience
explanation: Okafor concludes that the uneven ink shows an inexperienced printer. Text 2 calls that "unlikely." It agrees the ink is uneven but explains it as a deliberate wiping technique, because the same pattern shows up in all twelve prints. This choice matches that response.

A.why: You denied what both texts observe. Text 2 accepts that the skies fade and offers a different reason for it.

B.why: You picked an objection Text 2 never raises. Paper and dating aren't discussed. The disagreement is about what the uneven ink means.

C.why: You took a claim about technique too far. Text 2 says the fading was intentional. It says nothing about ranking the printer against other artisans.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the researchers' conclusion in Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Materials scientists coated steel plates with a new silica-based film and placed them in a salt-spray chamber that simulates seawater exposure. After six months, the coated plates showed no measurable rust, while uncoated plates were badly corroded. The researchers concluded that the film will protect steel bridges for decades.

Text 2
The chamber results are certainly impressive. But outdoor bridges also face sunlight, freezing, and constant flexing, none of which the chamber reproduced. A six-month indoor test cannot establish how the film will hold up over decades.
choices: By contending that the coated plates rusted in the chamber just as badly as the uncoated plates
By contending that a short indoor test does not show the film will protect bridges for decades
By contending that the film will most likely fail within a few years on outdoor steel bridges
By contending that the silica-based film is too expensive to apply to large steel bridges
explanation: Text 1 ends with the claim that the film will protect bridges for decades. Text 2 accepts the chamber results ("certainly impressive") and then turns: the test was short and left out real-world stresses, so it "cannot establish" decades of protection. Text 2 is saying the claim hasn't been shown, not that it is false.

A.why: You overlooked the concession. Text 2 calls the chamber results "impressive," so it accepts that the coated plates resisted rust.

C.why: You fell for the trap this question is built around. Text 2 says the test cannot show long-term protection. It doesn't predict that the film will fail, so this choice is too strong.

D.why: You picked an objection Text 2 never makes. Cost isn't mentioned. Text 2's concern is whether the test supports the long-term claim.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Materials scientists at a university lab developed a polymer coating that sealed fine scratches on steel within six hours at room temperature. Because the coating repairs itself, the team concluded that it could replace conventional protective paint on highway bridges.

Text 2
The coating's self-repair in the lab is impressive. Calling it a replacement for bridge paint, however, is premature. The lab never exposed it to freezing nights or road salt, which bridges face every winter.
choices: The coating is ready to replace the protective paint now used on bridges.
The coating sealed fine scratches on steel during the laboratory tests.
The coating breaks down when it is exposed to freezing nights and road salt.
Conventional bridge paint repairs its scratches more slowly than the coating.
explanation: Text 2 grants Text 1's lab result ("The coating's self-repair in the lab is impressive") and then rejects only the conclusion that it can replace bridge paint. The shared ground is the lab finding: the coating sealed fine scratches in testing.

A.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and it is exactly the claim Text 2 calls premature. You picked the point the two authors disagree on.

C.why: Text 2 says the coating was never tested in freezing weather or road salt, not that it fails under them. You read "hasn't been shown" as "proved wrong."

D.why: Neither text says how conventional paint handles scratches. You took a comparison the passages never make.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Historian Mara Ellison examined a surviving pattern book from an eighteenth-century weaving workshop and found that nearly all of its cloth samples are indigo blue. She concludes that the workshop's customers strongly preferred blue cloth.

Text 2
Ellison is right that indigo dominates the pattern book, but her conclusion is unlikely to hold. Indigo resists fading far better than most period dyes, so samples in other colors may simply have faded to a dull brown and been mistaken for undyed cloth.
choices: The workshop's customers strongly preferred blue cloth over other colors.
The workshop sold more cloth in other colors than it sold in indigo blue.
Resistance to fading was the main reason the weavers chose to use indigo.
Most of the cloth samples in the surviving pattern book appear indigo blue.
explanation: Text 2 accepts Ellison's observation ("indigo dominates the pattern book") and offers another explanation for it: other colors may have faded. Both authors therefore accept that the surviving samples are mostly blue.

A.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and Text 2 says it is "unlikely to hold." You chose the claim under attack instead of the shared observation.

B.why: Text 2 only says other colors *may* have faded. It never claims they outsold indigo. You took a possibility as proof of the opposite.

C.why: Text 2 mentions how well indigo resists fading to explain the pattern book, not to explain why weavers chose it. Neither author discusses the weavers' reasons.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a twelve-week study, adults who ate a high-fiber breakfast cereal every day lowered their LDL cholesterol by an average of 8 percent. The researchers therefore concluded that the cereal lowers cholesterol in adults of all ages.

Text 2
The study's results are encouraging, but its conclusion goes too far. Every participant was between 25 and 40 years old. Older adults process dietary fiber differently, so whether they would see the same benefit remains unknown.
choices: Participants in the study saw their LDL cholesterol decrease on average.
The cereal lowers LDL cholesterol in adults regardless of their age.
The cereal does not lower LDL cholesterol in adults older than 40.
Most of the participants in the study were older than 40 years of age.
explanation: Text 2 calls the results "encouraging," so it accepts the finding that LDL fell among participants. What it rejects is extending that finding to every age group. The drop in the study group is what both authors agree on.

B.why: This is Text 1's broad conclusion, which Text 2 says "goes too far." You chose the claim Text 2 narrows.

C.why: Text 2 says the effect in older adults "remains unknown," not that there is no effect. This choice is too strong for Text 2, and Text 1 would reject it anyway.

D.why: Text 2 says every participant was between 25 and 40. This choice reverses that.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
For eight weeks, one group of sprinters trained barefoot on grass while another trained in shoes on a synthetic track. The barefoot group cut more time from its 40-meter sprint. The coach who ran the study concluded that barefoot training strengthens foot muscles in ways that speed acceleration.

Text 2
The barefoot group did improve more. However, it also trained on a softer surface, and it is difficult to exclude the grass itself as the cause of the gain.
choices: Training barefoot strengthens the foot muscles that speed acceleration.
The grass surface, not barefoot training, caused the sprinters' gains.
The barefoot group improved its 40-meter times more than the other group.
Both groups of sprinters trained on the same synthetic track surface.
explanation: Text 2 opens by granting the result ("The barefoot group did improve more") and then challenges only the explanation for it. Both authors accept that the barefoot group gained more.

A.why: This is the coach's conclusion in Text 1, which Text 2 questions. You chose the explanation Text 2 doubts instead of the result both accept.

B.why: Text 2 only says the grass "is difficult to exclude" as a cause. It does not claim the grass was the cause. This choice is too strong.

D.why: Both texts say the barefoot group trained on grass and the shoe group trained on a synthetic track. This choice contradicts that.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
During the summer of 2025, a forecasting team's new model correctly predicted afternoon thunderstorms over a coastal region on 82 percent of days, compared with 70 percent for the older model. The team concluded that the new model should replace the older one in every season.

Text 2
While the new model clearly outperformed in summer, that success says little about winter. Winter storms there come from large frontal systems, not the local heating that drives summer storms.
choices: The new model should replace the older model in every season of the year.
The new model predicted summer thunderstorms more accurately than the older one.
The new model forecasts winter storms less accurately than the older one does.
Summer thunderstorms are the most damaging weather the coastal region faces.
explanation: Text 2 grants that "the new model clearly outperformed in summer" and then limits the scope: summer results don't tell us about winter. Both authors accept the summer finding.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion, and it is the claim Text 2 rejects. You chose the point the two authors disagree on.

C.why: Text 2 says the summer results say little about winter, not that the model does worse in winter. You turned "not shown" into "shown to be worse."

D.why: Neither text ranks how damaging the region's weather is. You chose a claim neither author makes.
